Andrew Kastl Andy 27 November 1853, Stara Hut, house No. 1, Bohemia Oboc, or the Old "Hut", Novo-Kdysky County, in the old Country 5 May 1906 Two years before the Katolik newspaper article was printed Plasi, Saunders County, Nebraska Barbara Valecka Arrived at Baltimore 29 May 1867, aged 13, with his brother Thomas The last child of his mother Maria, who died soon after his birth. The newspaper article says she died the day after he was born, and that he was the fourteenth and last child of the first marriage. Lived for some time with Peter Kastl after coming to America in 1867 (the article calls Peter first his brother, then his uncle); Peter found him farm work, which he did until he was 21 Homesteaded some land and dug out a hole in the bank for his home; later sold the property and moved to Wahoo Tavern business in Wahoo with a partner, who soon put him out; then farm work again, including several years with an Irish family Settled on school land with his brother Jakub County assessor for many years An article about his life, "Andrew Kastl, West Nebraska, and his large family", was printed in the Czech newspaper Katolik ("Katolika" in the book's introduction), Chicago, probably in 1904. The article says two of his daughters were married, "one to T. Rech and one to Joe Vrbka".

Jacob Kastl Jakub Kastl, Jakob Kastl, Grandpa Kastl 5 May 1847, Všepadly, house No. 11, Bohemia 25 July 1847, Ouboc 28 February 1935, at the home of his son Frank Plasi, Saunders County, Nebraska Alzbeta Nemecek; marriage contract signed 31 January 1872, Lepadlech, Bohemia 1872, with his new bride Son of Thomas Kastl and Maria, the daughter of Joseph Marselek (so spelled here), a magistrate manager from Kosenice; Thomas and Maria were farmers near Všepadly The 1872 marriage agreement names him son of Tomas Kastl, a small farmer from Old Hutti (the typed translation is faint here) By the marriage agreement his bride was to bring him 500 zlatych, and her father Joseph Nemecek was to give him 250 zlatych to prepare for a trip to America A farm near Plasi, Saunders County, Nebraska, some three months after he and his wife emigrated in 1872 Near Plasi, Saunders County, for some time, then east Butler County, Nebraska; for his last 23 years at the home of his son Frank, near Bruno A devout Catholic and one of the founders of the first Catholic church at Plasi; a member of the K.D. Lodge; in later years one of his pastimes was singing Died after an illness of two weeks, in his 87th year. Funeral at the Plasi Catholic church, Monday 4 March 1935; the pallbearers were his four sons John, Vincent, Frank and Anton, and two nephews, Charles Kastl of Prague and Thomas Kastl of North Bend His obituary says eleven children were born to him and his wife, four of whom (Louis, Ann, Jake and Ed) died before him; 28 grandchildren and five great-grandchildren survived him

Baltimore, from Bremen Arrived 14 August 1872 on the S.S. Berlin Son of Thomas Kastl, a farmer, and Maria, the daughter of Joseph Marselek (so spelled here), a magistrate manager from Kosenice Applied 13 September 1872 at Lincoln, Nebraska, for 80 acres in Elk Precinct, Saunders County (west half of the southeast quarter of Section 30, Township 15 North, Range 5 East), near the site of Sts. Cyril and Methodius Church (Plasi); proof of homestead dated 11 March 1879; final certificate 13 March 1879 Received his certificate of U.S. citizenship 16 October 1878 Farmer; postmaster of a station called Newton, a mail center on his farmstead (Newton never became an incorporated village) It is not known whether the family stopped in Chicago (the ship records give it as destination), Iowa or Wisconsin before coming to Nebraska Lived on the farm until his death at age 55

pages.h: Preface
pages.t:
## Preface

This family history came about through the efforts of many people. A few years ago several Kastl descendants, unknown to each other, began to think about their heritage, and collected bits and pieces of material; photographs, stories, records of birth and marriages, cemetery marker statistics, etc. Fortunately, some of these relatives, distant as they were, found each other and began to coordinate the findings, and the idea of a family history began. Perhaps there can never be a complete list of all the descendants of the seven Kastl brothers, and the family of one half-sister who came to America, but at least it is a beginning. Hopefully, there will be someone some day who may wish and be able to continue and expand this project.

So many sources were used it is difficult to name them all. Family records, reminiscences (some collected on tape), and photographs have been most important; also letters, visits, and phone calls were all useful. The Plasi Church records were examined. Census records, old newspaper items, homestead applications, ship passenger lists, birth and death dates, etc. — all were checked during trips to Nebraska State Historical Society Library, Omaha Public Library, National Archives in Washington, D. C., California State records, County Courthouses, and cemeteries. The genealogical records from the Archives in Plzen, Czechoslovakia were received from correspondence through the Czech Embassy in Washington. With these records it has been possible to trace ancestors for several generations back, and have a picture of where they lived and what they did.

It is hoped that most of the information here is correct, or nearly so. Apologies are made for any errors, omissions, or inconsistencies. Many letters have been written to relatives for information. For the most part, they were answered with family lists and were greatly appreciated. So many people have helped in the preparation of this history that they cannot all be acknowledged individually. But every bit of information was useful and necessary, and this history could not have been prepared with out the help of all.

Acknowledgement and thanks are given to all of those who responded with interest and family information. To those who wished family names not to be included, and to those who did not respond, acknowlledgement {sic} is also given with respect to their privacy.

And, our thanks go to Father Jerome Pokorny and Delores Strizek of the Catholic Quote for their help in getting this book into print.

Evelyn Coufal
Francis Vech

pages.h: How To Use The Book
pages.t:
## How To Use The Book

There is no simple and perfect system for arranging and numbering family groups. And no matter what system is used, there will be difficulty in following it, and someone will find fault with it.

There is no consecutive numbering system in this book. Nor, are Roman numerals or letters of the alphabet used.

There is a separate chapter for each of the seven Kastl brothers, and one for the half-sister from Thomas Kastl's second family. The first list in each chapter are names of the children of the Kastl brother (or sister). Following are lists of families of these children and those descending from them. After the name of each child in this "first" generation, in parenthesis, are the father's (or mother's) name, and the ancestors in Bohemia which appeared in the early records from the Plzen Archives. These include Thomas, the father of the seven brothers and half-sister and continue back to the earliest known Kastl in the line. Like this: Peter's son Charles would be listed as CHARLES KASTL (Peter, Thomas, John, John, Andreas); showing Charles was the son of Peter, who was the son of Thomas, who was the son of John, who was the son of John, who was the son of Andreas. On succeeding generations, however, the four oldest ancestors are omitted (to keep the list from getting too long and repetitious) and only the names going back to the original brother or half-sister appear. For example: Peter. Charles's daughter would be listed as LILLIAN KASTL (Charles, Peter); Lillian's son would be FRANCIS VECH (Lillian Kastl Vech, Charles, Peter) — this shows Francis's Mother, Grandfather, and Great Grandfather. It can be assumed if no last name appears in the parenthesis, it is a Kastl.

Succeeding pages within the family group, list following generations with as much information as has been collected.

By opening the book at any page, one can tell which family the descendant is from by checking the first name in the parenthesis which is the parent, and then on back to the original Kastl brother, or half-sister, which is the last name in the parenthesis.

Abbreviations used are b — born; m — married; d — died; bur — buried; div — divorced; aka — also known as.

No attempt has been made to standardize the spelling of names. Sometimes they appear in the Czech spelling, often in the American version. Therefore, interchangeably, will be found Wenceslaus, Wenzel, Vaclav, Alzbeta, Elizabeth, Jacob, Jakub, Jakob, Jan, John, Alois, Louis, etc.

pages.h: A Brief History of Czechoslovakia
pages.t:
## A Brief History of Czechoslovakia

## (Bohemia—Moravia)

September 11, 1918, British Prime Minister, Lloyd George telegraphed to Professor Masaryk, President of the Czech National Council, "Your nation has rendered inestimable service to Russia and to the Allies in this struggle to free the world from despotism. We shall never forget it." On September 27, 1938, twenty years later, Prime Minister Chamberlain, broadcasting to the British Empire, tried to justify the surrender of Czechoslovakia to Nazi Germany, by describing the Czechs as "people of whom we know nothing."

Years from now our descendants may say of our ancestors; we know nothing. This is an attempt to preserve a geneological history of a certain Kastl family. Some legends, some facts — the truth may lie somewhere in between.

The Kastl family seems to have originated in Austria, then migrated to Bohemia, possibly in the 1600's. The name Bohemia comes from the Celtic Boii — a combination of Boian and Marcoman — of Celtic and Teutonic blood. Legend gave the name Cech to their first mythical leader. The real date of Bohemia starts in the ninth century. The first Czech chronicler was a man named Cosmos.

The first migration of Czechs to their present home in Europe is assigned to the fifth century. They were followed by a non Aryan tribe, the Avars, who settled in Hungary. In the eighth century there was organized a national Czech dynasty headed by the Premysl family. They ruled for five centuries until 1306. This was one of the first national states of Europe. In the ninth century, Moravia took the place of Bohemia under two princes, Mojmer and Rostislav. A long series of struggles against Germanic invasions began. At this time, the medieval Church played a great part in the colonization of Eastern Europe.

In 863, Rostislav is described as a heathen monarch. The forces of Christianity were closing in on his domain. The missionaries of the west with whom Christianity and Germanism went hand in hand were a menace to his survival. He then cast his hand with the Byzantine Empire appealing for clergy capable of expounding the Christian faith in the language of the country. Two missionaries were sent: Cyril and Methodius. They were acquainted with the slav dialects and are credited with the invention of a new slavonic script. There was considerable friction between the eastern and western branches of the Church.

Prince Vaclav (Wenseslaus) of Bohemia, was a pious Czech Christian leader, but his religion, and his treaty with the Germans, caused discontent among the nobles. He was assassinated by his own brother in 929. Later he was recognized as the patron Saint Wenceslaus of Bohemia, and became a legend after his death — and more familiar to us perhaps, as the "Good King Wenceslaus" in the English Christmas carol.

Byzantine influence proved to be too remote to assert itself and Bohemia/Moravia came under the influence of Rome. In 1306, Wenceslaus III, last King of the Premyslide dynasty, was murdered. His death created a vacuum as there were no male heirs left. Elizabeth, sister of Wenceslaus III, had married John of Luxemburg, and he was chosen King of Bohemia in 1310. Thus, the house of Luxemburg became the next rulers of Bohemia. Prince Charles, the son of John and Elizabeth, at age 30 acquired two crowns, Germanic and Bohemian. In 1355, he, as Charles IV, became emporer of the Holy Roman Empire, thus giving Bohemia the honor of furnishing one of the Holy Roman Emporers.

Under Charles's reign, reforms were made in education, and in 1348, he signed the Charter of Prague University, the first university of its kind in Central Europe. The students of the middle ages were a mixture of rich and poor, and from different countries. Every class and age came to the University of Prague. Prague rapidly became a culture center. At this time the Cathedral of St. Vitus was started. Also, the Charles bridge was built. It is the most famous bridge surviving medieval times. This period was referred to as the Golden Age — 1346-1378.

The following years became a period of turmoil and disputes. Marked by inept leadership of various kings of Europe, the Church was divided between two Popes, one in Rome, Gregory XII, one in Avignon, France, Benedict XIII. There was considerable abuse in the administration of Church affairs. The Council of Pisa in 1409 deposed both Popes and elected Greek Alexander V, and for a short time there were three Popes. At this time there appeared on the scene in Bohemia, John Huss, a Czech religious reformer.

Of peasant origin, John Huss studied theology at the University of Prague and was ordained a priest. The Church in Bohemia had become wealthy, and somewhat corrupt, as the leadership strayed from its ideals. Reformers came from within the clergy, and young John Huss preached for the reform of the abuses of the clergy. He gained only hostility from the Church, was excommunicated, and in 1415, burned at the stake. For the next 15 years, the Kingdom of Bohemia underwent a devastating period known as the Hussite Wars, with clashes between radical and moderate factions. The moderates returned to the Catholic Church, but Bo-

hemia/Moravia was technically a Protestant state.

Unrest in Bohemia/Moravia continued, and for the next hundred years, the crown was passed from Hapsburgs to Hungarians, and back again, and the Czech people suffered. They were being deprived of self rule, and the peasants reduced to virtual serfdom.

In 1620, the Czech Protestants revolted, and clashed with the imperial Hapsburg Army on Bila Hora (White Mountain) near Prague, The Czechs lost the battle, and the independance of Bohemia ended for 300 years. This was a sad and historic moment in the existence of the Czech nation.

The loss of the Czech nobility, both on the battlefield and later in executions and exile, was a deep blow to the nationalism of the Czech people. German speaking Austrians replaced the lost native Czech leaders and nobility, and for over two centuries the Hapsburgs dominated the area. The German language replaced the Czech in the administration, culture, and education. Only in the fields of the peasants and among the common workers did the Czech language survive. This was, indeed, a very dark period for a once fiercely proud and advanced nation.

During this time the lands became consolidated under the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Provinces including Bohemia and Moravia, and at some times, Poland, and what we know now as Austria and Hungary, were under the Hapsburg rule. The people were subjects of the Austrian crown, and that is why the Czech immigrants arriving in the United States put as their nationality, Austrian.

By the early nineteenth century the Czech people began a gradual rebirth of nationalism — slowly there was a revival of the language and culture. The Austrian rulers, however, still controlled the provinces and the repressive measures (enumerated in "The Kastls: from Bohemia to America") forced many Czech people to decide to emigrate to the United States. And, we now come to the period in Czech history when our Kastl ancestors joined that movement to leave their homeland.

It was not until 1918, after the First World War, that Czechoslovakia finally gained its independence. Thomas G. Massaryk was its first president. Bohemia and Moravia, together with the provinces of Selesia and Slovakia were joined together to make the modern state of Czechoslovakia as we know it today. At least, geographically.

pages.h: Map
The Kastls
pages.t:
## The Kastls

## from Bohemia to America

There were seven Kastl brothers who left Bohemia and came to America. They were from an area south and a little west of Plzen. Villages mentioned in accounts of the time were Vsepadly, Stars Hut, and Nova Kdnye. The brothers were Peter, Wenzel (James), Jan (John), Joseph, Jakub, Thomas, and Andrew; the sons of a farmer, Thomas, and his wife Maria Maraslek.

The first Kastl for which there is a record is one Andress Kastl (1). Nothing is known about Andreas and his wife Margarita except that their names appear on the birth record as parents of Wolfgang Jan Kastl (2). Born 29, October 1742, at Hradiste. The birth record of Wolfgang Jan is the oldest record to come from the Archives in Czechoslovakia. (The early records were in Latin. Several of the later ones in the registers were recorded in German, which was the official language at the time when Bohemia was a part of the Austrian Empire).

Wolfgang Jan Kastl was a farmer at Hradiste, with his wife Barbara, when their son Jan Kastl (3). was born 13 March 1777, at Hradiste, house no. 11.

Jan Kastl, a carpenter living in Hradiste, married Maria, daughter of Andreas Muzik, a farmer from Vsepadly, house no. 11, on 10 February 1801. Their son Thomas (4). was born 15 September 1806, at Vsepadly. He became a farmer and married Maria, daughter of Joseph Marsalek, a magistrate manager at Kosenice, no. 33, on 30 January 1827. These were the parents of the seven brothers who came to America in the 1800s. There may have been a daughter, Eva. She is mentioned in the obituary of Jacob Kastl as a sister who preceded him in death. To date, nothing has been found to verify this.

Maria Marsalek Kastl, mother of the seven brothers, died when Andrew, the youngest was born in November 1853. (A story, handed down through the generations is that as the m other looked upon her newborn son, and knowing she could not live, said, "Who will take care of you.") Thomas Kastl took a second wife. On 6 February 1855, at Vsepadly, house No. 3, he married 26 year old Barbara Kellner, daughter of Simon Kellner of Vsepadly. Thomas was then 48 years old. (Another story handed down is that Barbara had been the girlfriend of Peter, the eldest son of Thomas. But while Peter was off fighting with the Austrian Army, his father took her as his bride). Six children were born to Thomas and Barbara Kellner Kastl. They were Alzbeta (died in infancy), Marie, Frances, Anna, Joseph, and Alzbeta. According to the records, Thomas Kastl fathered 14 children; two in the second family died, one an infant, the other 6 years old. The only descendant of the second family to come to America was James Zima.

The above vital statistics came from the Plzen, Czechoslovakia Archives which house records of births and marriages, and since these ancestors were Roman Catholics, the Church records provided the information.

Peter Kastl was the first brother to come to America, and one by one the others followed. Some had families, but others were still very young men. Peter, John, Jakub, and Andrew were buried in Nebraska in the country cemetery of Sts. Cyril and Methodius Church, also know as Plasi in Saunders County, Nebraska. Joseph was buried at Brainard, Nebraska; Wenzel at Omaha, and Thomas in Illinois.

The final abolition of Serfdom in 1849, over population in the country-side, 1848 revolt against Austrian rule ruthlessly crushed, passive resistance in 1863, the defeat of the Habsburg Government (Franz Joseph) in the Austro Prussian war 1866 resulting in the occupation of Prague by Prussian Troops, Martial Law invoked in 1868, military conscription; these were the reasons for immigration.

Railroads advertising cheap land, the Homestead Law of 1862, the end of the war between the states; these were some of the reasons they chose America.

Leaving their small villages they left by train for Bremen, Germany where they boarded ship, arriving in Baltimore in three or four weeks. We were successful in obtaining ship records on John, Joseph, Wenzel, Thomas, and Andrew. We did not find any records on Peter or Jakob.

Peter was the first to leave. The year is unclear. Grandmother Anna Frohner Kastl told her grandchildren that Abe Lincoln was assassinated (April 14, 1865) while they were on a train coming west. Andreas' History of Nebraska, Volume II, page 1400, states Peter came in 1866. With Peter and his wife Anna were three children: Anna, Joseph, and Mary. The next to arrive May 29, 1867, were Andrew, age 13 and Thomas, age 17. They came on the ship SS Johanne Wilhelmine. On October 2, 1867, Wenzel; wife Barbara and three children John, Martin, and Wenzel arrived on the ship SS Humbolt. Following Wenzel was Joseph, wife Dorothea and two children Mathias and Theresia, arriving April 22, 1868, on the ship SS Berlin. The last two brothers, John and Jakob, arrived in 1872. John's date of arrival was August 14. With him were his wife, Marie, children: Wenzel 8, Barbara 6, Anna 3, and Josef 11 months. They sailed on the ship SS Berlin. Jakob came with his new bride some time in April 1872.

pages.h: Joseph Kastl log house built 1868.
pages.t:
Five of the brothers came prior to transcontinental train travel which occurred in 1869. The Chicago Northwestern reached Council Bluffs in 1867. Passengers crossed the Missouri River by ferry to Omaha. In 1866 the Union Pacific Railroad was well on its way spanning Nebraska from east to west. The Union Pacific began its railroad from Omaha west before the Chicago Northwestern reached Council Bluffs from the east. Trains were brought by barge up the Missouri River for the Union Pacific. Our people came west by train as far as Fremont or North Bend, Nebraska, where they forded and Platte River into Saunders County.

Peter, the oldest and the first to leave Bohemia, was an officer in the Austrian Army. (He served his time and then the authorities wanted him back in the army so he made a hasty departure to America.) He first went to Racine, Wisconsin where there was a Czech settlement. In 1866 he was in Cedar Rapids, Iowa where he worked in the building trade. On June 26, 1867 Peter was in Nebraska City where he filed for a homestead.

Peter Kastl was the first Czech settler to apply for homestead in the Butler—Saunders County area. He was the first settler in Elk precinct—Saunders County and the first Czech in Butler and Saunders Counties. His application number was 1395. Cost was fourteen dollars. This was on Section 21, Township 13 North, Range 4, East 160 acres. At this same time he pre-empted 80 acres, pre-emption Certificate 837, West ½ of Southeast ¼, Section 22, Range 4 East, Township 13 North. Cost was $1.25 per acre. This land was in Butler County, Nebraska. On May 1, 1868 Peter pre-empted 80 acres, pre-emption Certificate 1163, N½ SE¼ Section 20, Township 15 North, Range 5 East. Cost was $2.50 per acre. This is the land where Peter settled in the Plasi vicinity.

The land that he homesteaded in Butler County was relinquished in 1869. This was done for these reasons. There was a certain amount of timber in the area around Plasi, a number of springs feed the small creeks in the area, and also more land was available for further Czech settlers who he knew were soon to come.

The original homestead was near an area called the speculator tract. This was a large amount of land which was held for a time by eastern investors.

Andrew and Thomas, ages 13 and 17, were the next to arrive. An account of Andrew's life is reprinted from a newspaper article written in the early 1900s. Thomas eventually settled in Champaign, Illinois, where he had a buggy factory.



Joseph came to America April 22, 1868. On June 20, 1868, he filed for homestead at the land office in Nebraska City. Application number was 2069. Description of the land was E½ of the SE¼. Section 4, Township 14 North, 80 acres in Newman Precinct. July 6, 1875, in his final proof required under the homestead act, Joseph states he built a house of logs, 16x32, with two doors and four windows. The remains of this log house are still visible on the original site. The State Historical Society in Lincoln, Nebraska, has on file pictures and notes of this particular log house. They describe it as follows: Joseph Kastl log house built 1868.

pages.h: Joseph Kastl log house built 1868 — new siding put on at a later date.
pages.t:
". . . it may have been a combination of oak and cottonwood. Some of the logs have withstood weathering quite well and these may be oak. Others are in an advance state of deterioration, which leads me to think that they may be of cottonwood.

"Relative to the clay plaster, we do not have a scientific analysis of its contents. Typically, however, local clay would be mixed with small quantities of straw and occasionally manure to a rather thick consistency for use in plaster. This material is quite durable, as long as it stays dry. In many cases, a later coat of lime plaster was laid over the clay. Lath for the Kastl house consisted of small wooden pegs driven into the logs. I have only recorded this technique on one other building, a Czech log house in Knox County.

"The Kastl house, like many other Czech log houses that we have recorded, was one of the finest examples of the art of log building in the State of Nebraska. The Czechs were quite skilled in these techniques and are noted for their ability to build tight, chinkless walls (little or no space between logs), and finely — crafted corner notches. The Kastl house notches, while almost "square", are really a "ful-dovetail" notch, the most difficult notch to craft of any built in the United States. Other notable features include the mortised ceiling beams, and the mortised door and window jambs (the vertical posts on either side) which accept tenoned logs on either side."

Peter Kastl also built a log house, 18x20. According to the Land Certificates, the log cabins were built in 1868.

A biographical sketch of John and Jakub, the sixth and seventh brothers to arrive, can be found in the beginning of the chapters on John's and Jakob's descendants. Joseph Kastl log house built 1868 — new siding put on at a later date.

pages.h: The Kastls in Pioneer Nebraska
pages.t:
## The Kastls in Pioneer Nebraska

At the beginning of settlement in Nebraska, the terminology "The Great American Desert" was often used in describing the area west of the Missouri River. Immigrant settlers often heard this expression as they broke the prarie moving steadily westward. The imaginary "desert line" moved with the line of settlement by those who were determined to have a desert. Eventually Nebraska was completely settled and the desert idea disappeared. In later years, Nebraska was referred to as the "White spot of the Nation", also "The garden spot of the Nation." The first settlers must have been men and women who could meet a crisis with strong courage, and survive on determination and hard work.

The progress of Butler and Saunders Counties previous to the spring of 1869, was very slow. Population of Butler and Saunders County was estimated at 400 in 1867. The first census report was in 1870.

From the later 1840s to the start of the war between the states in 1861, there had been a great deal of wagon train traffic along both sides of the Platte river, the destination being in most cases, the western gold fields or the Morman settlement in Utah. There was also military activity as they established trails and forts. The routes along the Platte River were largely settled by wagon train dropouts. They established ranches, a term used for early day motels, a place to obtain rest and supplies.

Early settlement of Saunders County occurred around the old California road, which ran from Nebraska City through Saline Ford (Ashland), through Saunders and Butler Counties to (Columbus) and then to Fort Kearney. This was also referred to as the "Ox Bow Trail."

Along the bluffs, south of the Platte River and east of the town of Cedar Bluffs, the Chrilton expedition of seven families homesteaded land in 1865. Peter Carstensen settled in this area in 1866 and his son, Ness, was one of the first white children born in this area in 1869. Ness Carstensen wrote an interesting account of his life before he died in 1960. John Garret, who settled in the same area, came very early in 1861. It was from him, that my Great Grandfather Peter Kastl bought supplies, and obtained advice and direction as to where his homestead was located.

Our account of the Kastl brothers' life in Nebraska begins in 1867, the year Nebraska became a state. Peter Kastl, the first brother to arrive, came as far as Council Bluffs, Iowa, in 1867, by train from Cedar Rapids, Iowa. With him were his wife and four children. They crossed the river by ferry to Omaha, Nebraska, where there was a small Czech settlement. Peter was fluent in speaking the German language (in the dialect spoken by the Austrians). He also had some knowledge of English words, but the family preferred the Czech language. From Omaha, Peter went to Nebraska City, probably by paddle wheel steamboat that served the area at that time, to file for his homestead. He then returned to Omaha, and from there left by train for Fremont, Nebraska, and there he crossed the Platte River into Saunders County. He then walked, following the old Pawnee Indian trail along the bluffs of the Platte River, a distance of about twenty five miles to a small settlement, where Linwood is now located. This was also the site of the first Post Office in the area. From this spot, Peter had to travel about twenty five miles south in Butler County, to his first homestead. The area there was not to his liking, and he eventually settled in the area around Plasi.

On the Ed Havorka farm, three miles southeast of Linwood, stands a roadside cross. Historical tradition has it that this cross was erected by Czech settlers. Some say this was a gathering place for prayer services. Others say it was a directional sign. It may have been both. From this cross, ten miles south, is where Peter eventually settled. This was the site of the first Czech settlement in Saunders and Butler Counties and was called Pilzen, which later was changed to Plasi.

It was here in Section 20, Elk Precinct, that Peter first built a dugout, a place to live, until he finished his log house in 1868. BY then, there were five children. Thomas was born in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, and Philomena was probably born in Omaha, February 9, 1868. Peter's youngest brother, Andrew, who came from Bohemia in 1867, also lived with the family. The families of Wenzel and Joseph lived in Omaha while the men were erecting their log houses. It was during this time that Joseph's children, Matthias and Theresa, both died, and were buried in Omaha.

Peters first neighbor in Elk Precinct was an old Pawnee Indian who refused to go to the Indian Reservation near what is now Genoa, Nebraska. The Reservation had been established in the 1850s. Peter tried to interest him in attending prayer services or Sunday Mass, which a priest would come to offer four or five times a year. The first Mass in that locality was offered in 1870 at the home of Joseph Simanek. The Pawnee would always manage to be busy on Sundays, but the rest of the week was spent in watching Peter do his work. The Pawnee Indians would often visit this area. One of their ancestral homes and burial grounds was near Linwood. They would travel the high grounds, a habit they developed from conflict with the Sioux. The Pawnee were always friendly. The Kastl family raised a type of

pages.h: Map

pages.t:
sorghum from which they made molasses, and would share this with the Indians.

The years from 1867 to 1882 were a time of improving the homesteads and acquiring stock and primitive machinery. The pioneers broke the prairie and planted fruit trees, fought grasshoppers, and prairie fires. In 1870 a large prairie fire swept through Butler County and parts of Saunders County, destroying crops, livestock, and buildings. This area was also on the trail of the longhorn cattle drives that originated at Bandero, Texas, their destination being the railroad at Schuyler, Nebraska. In April of 1872, there was a herd of about 2000 of these cattle bedded down in southern Butler County. That same evening, a torrential rain occurred with periodical lightning, causing the cattle to stampede for twenty five miles in all directions. The settlers in the area then butchered many of the cattle. This was the last large trail drive to Schuyler. They then moved the drives further west to North Platte. In March of 1870, the Herd Law was passed by the Nebraska Legislature. It required stockmen to fence cattle in, rather than requiring grain growers to fence them out. Barbed wire was patented in 1874.

The first school district in Elk Precinct was organized in 1869, and a sod schoolhouse was erected. J. P. Dunlap taught the first school term that winter. Mr. Dunlap settled in Newman Precinct in 1867. He later married Christina Campbell, daughter of Peter Campbell, who, along with her sister and two brothers, were taken prisoners by a band of Ogallala Sioux on July 24, 1867. The Campbells, at this time, had a homestead south of Grand Island, where Doniphan is now located. Government authorities negotiated with the Indians and secured their release. They were held by the Indians for more than two months. In the spring of 1868, the Campbell family abandoned their homestead and moved to Saunders County.

An interesting event in this period of time was the slaughter of the buffalo. In the 1870s it was estimated that 10,000,000 were killed. The line of the buffalo range was west of Grand Island. In January of 1872, the Grand Duke Alexis of Russia staged his famous buffalo hunt with Buffalo Bill Cody as his chief guide. Five hundred people left from North Platte, which included troops, teamsters, cooks, skinners, servants, and friends of the Duke. The hunt was staged southwest of North Platte.

The Sioux and Cheyenne Indian uprisings, although not affecting eastern Nebraska, were on the minds of many settlers. Frank and Luther North were instrumental in organizing the Pawnee Scouts and together with the U.S. Army, subdued the Indian uprisings. The Battle of the Big Horn, where General Custer and his command were wiped out, occurred in July 1876. Jesse James and other notorious outlaws applied their trade throughout the plains area.

During this period of glamorous history, it is doubtful much attention was paid to it by Czech settlers, their interest being in survival. Ashland was the nearest mill, established in 1864. Nebraska City was the first market for grain.

A trip to Nebraska City by Peter and Joseph was made in 1870. They had raised some corn, a little more than they thought they needed. They decided to market the corn in Nebraska City where they would receive the highest price. The distance traveled would be about one hundred miles each way. There were two wagon loads of corn, thirty bushels in each wagon, drawn by oxen. When they arrived, they unloaded the corn, and sat in a small building waiting for their money. They opened the door and saw their oxen headed down the road a quarter of a mile away. Someone had started the oxen with the idea of fleecing the settlers. After catching up with the oxen, Joseph, being outspoken and short tempered, took matters in his own hands. He went back with his black snake whip and shotgun, and in strong broken English demanded the money for the corn. He was quickly paid and Peter and Joseph were on their way home. Later, markets were established when wagon bridges were built across the Platte River to North Bend and Fremont, which were on the Union Pacific Railroad.

In the late 1870s, there was a higher than normal rainfall. The educated and the intellectual people now dropped the desert theory. As they observed, and advised, and watched the desert bloom with corn, wheat, gardens, and fruit trees, they theorized that rain followed the plow, and tree planting drew moisture. The noise of the trains disturbed the atmospheric pressure which created more moisture.

Every pioneer had a flock of chickens which were necessary but were a problem as they were destructive to gardens and new seedlings. The Nebraska Farmer magazine in 1881, recommended the shoeing of hens by placing small woolen bags tied over their feet.

The 1880s marked a period of time when it became easier for the pioneers. The railroads came into the Saunders County towns which were being established, and by the middle 1880s, the rush was on to settle the rest of the State.

pages.h: The Kastls in California and Oklahoma
pages.t:
## The Kastls in California and Oklahoma

Of interest to the writers of this history was the migration of second generation Kastls to California and Oklahoma to obtain homesteads or cheap land.

Mary Kastl, the second daughter of Peter Kastl, born 1865 in Bohemia, married Joseph Cuda at Plasi, Nebraska, January 1887. That same year they moved to Hanford, California. The following year, 1888, Joseph Cuda homesteaded 160 acres of land in the San Joaquin Valley, Kern County, California. We have reprinted various newspaper articles which were printed about this pioneer family.

Joseph Kastl, first son of Peter Kastl, born 1863 in Bohemia, married Mary Fujan, September 1887. On March 30, 1899, the Joseph Kastl family moved to Kern County, California, and purchased land very near the Joseph Cuda homestead.

Mary B. Kastl, the first daughter of Jacob Kastl, born March 1873, married Vaclav Dobry April 1891, and that same year they moved to the Oklahoma Territory. This was the time of the opening of the Indian lands for settlement.

John J. Kastl, first son of Jacob Kastl, married Frances Policky in June 1902, and moved to the Oklahoma Territory. John J. Kastl purchased land near the Vaclav Dobry's.

Anton P. Kastl moved to the Oklahoma Territory sometime in the early 1900s. There he married Julia Hanska in 1908, and also purchased land in the area. Many other Czech families moved to the area, and soon the town of Yukon was founded and is known as the Czech capital of Oklahoma.

During the dust bowl and depression days of the 1930s, many people of the surrounding area left their farms in Oklahoma, and went to the San Joaquin Valley, and other parts of California looking for work in fruit orchards and grape fields. Some camped along the irrigation canals near the Cuda and Kastl ranches. All the livestock had to be locked up as nothing was safe as the newscomers were destitute and would steal if hungry. The Czech people of the Yukon area did not leave Oklahoma, however, and managed to hold on to their property until better times came. Today, as you drive through the area you see many oil wells and well-kept farmsteads.

The following are selected newspaper items from the Wahoo News Era in the 1890s.

August 24, 1893

Rudolph Kavalec killed Louis Kastl of Brainard last Sunday. They became engaged in a quarrel in front of Morris' saloon, when the former struck the latter in the neck with his fist causing instant death. The boys are aged respectively 17 and 18 years. Kastl is a son of Jacob Kastl of this county.

Bit by a Rattler — April 23, 1896

A little two year old child of Frank Kastl, living four miles southwest of town while playing on the porch last Saturday afternoon was bitten by a rattle snake. The snake crawled upon the porch where the child was at play.

The father brought the little one to the city as quickly as possible and all was done for it that medical aid could devise but to no effect, and the little one died about 7 o'clock on Saturday evening. It was buried Monday afternoon.

October 9, 1890

The democrats met last Friday at the court house and held their convention, and nominated G. W. Simpson for county attorney, John Lehmkuhl for county commissioner, Peter Kastl and E. Biggerstaff for representatives. This paper knows nothing against Mr. Kastl other than he was nominated to catch the Bohemian vote and Mr. Biggerstaff to catch any vote he can.

Mr. Lehmhuhl is a farmer but lives here in Wahoo and his connection with the banks places him beyond the support of the farmer.

Mr. Simpson has been county attorney for two years and his record is not the kind of a recommend a man would like to go before the people with.

In all the cases for the state he has been concerned in, not a single one has he been successful in, if he has this paper will gladly mention it. Now he has either been on the weak side or else had not the ability to conduct the cases. The ticket may be entirely satisfactory to a majority of the democrats but it is just the kind of a ticket for the independents to snow under on the 4th of November.

November 6, 1890

Peter Kastl and Walter Fleming will continue to be private citizens and move along farm life while Mr. Olson and Mr. Goffin represent glorious old Saunders County in the legislature this winter.

September 10, 1891

Joe Kastl, Chapman Precinct, was in Wahoo Saturday. He is running a thresher this fall and reports the yields of grain in parts of the county where he has been — as being on an average pretty good.

## The Family of Peter Kastl

"Peter Kastl, farmer, Section 20, P. O. Pilzen, was born in Bohemia November 1, 1827. He emigrated to America in 1866, and located at Cedar Rapids, Iowa,



where he resided until June 1867, when he came to Nebraska and located on the place where he now lives.

"He was the first settler in the Elk Precinct, and the first Bohemia settler in Saunders County. He and his wife were among the original members of the Catholic Church in that precinct, now the largest Catholic Church society in the county, which was organized in 1872 with a class of 65 members, at the same time took up a subscription to build a church, which funds reached $120 in cash, with which they bought 40 acres of land for church building and cemetery, said piece of land being plowed in one day by 60 men voluntarily with their teams.

"In 1878 they erected their present church, a fine large building, well furnished, with a capacity of 300 persons — size 72x40. The church also has large bell that can be heard miles away.

"He was married in Bohemia January 1859 to Miss Anna Frohner, who was born in Bohemia, June 21, 1839, by whom he has eight children, seven of whom are now living. He now owns 1040 acres of land in Butler and Saunders Counties, and started with only $1000.00"

From "History of the State of Nebraska," 1882. Vol. 2. Copyright 1975. Page 400.

pages.h: Joe Cuda Raised Pigs on Figs; Grew First Kern County Grapes
pages.t:
## Joe Cuda Raised Pigs on Figs; Grew First Kern County Grapes

(The Lamont Reporter—Dec. 31, 1959)

Among the first permanent settlers in this area were Mr. and Mrs. Joe Cuda. They had a wheat farm midway between the present sites of Arvin and Lamont as early as 1888.

Mr. Cuda was born in Bohemia in 1864, coming to the United States with his parents at the age of four. The Cudas lived in Nebraska, then moved to Tulare. When the Cudas came to the Vineland area the east Side Ditch was still in the talking stage.

With confidence in the area and the building of the canal in mind, the young pioneer farmer planted eight acres to Adriatic figs and seven acres to early and late Crawford peaches.

Until the ditch was completed and bringing life-giving waters to the farm, Cuda hauled water for his crops from a well on his property.

As the fig crop matured, Cuda would shake the fig trees to loosen the ripened figs. Elderly Indians of the Yokut Tribe at Tejon Ranch would gather up the fallen fruit and be paid by each boxfull they picked up.

Most of the figs were fed to the Cuda pigs and Cuda pork sold at a premium in Bakersfield butcher shops. The meat was described as "sweet and white, like turkey meat," by Joe Cuda's daughter, Helen, who lives at 1315 Quincy Street, Bakersfield.

Mayor Toomy of Fresno later bought the annual fig crop for his packing plant and the pigs got only the culls.

It was Joe Cuda and the father of Elza Foust who planted the first vineyard in Kern County on the Joe Smith Ranch. Smith was a well-known Bakersfield blacksmith. The first grapes were of the Muscat variety. Later Cuda planted 40 acres to seedless grapes and 35 acres to Elberta peaches as well as acres to hay, alfalfa, and corn.

He was active in forming the first Vineland School District and helped organize the Sunday afternoon jackrabbit drives to stamp out what had become a costly pest to the farmers in the area.

There were two Cuda children, Helen and Frank. The latter, now deceased, was an oilman who helped bring in the first U.S. Naval Reserve oil well in Wyoming. The wells were highlighted during the Harding administration in the "Teapot Dome Scandal" that shook Washington.

Helen Cuda was enrolled at Vineland School in 1897 and recalls the Jack, Tom and John Fowler families all living in the area as well as the Langdons. Laura Fowler, still in the area, is now Laura Russell. Miss CUda {sic} remembers trips into Bakersfield with the two-horse wagon loaded with wheat for the Kern Land Co. mill on Truxton Avenue. A Mr. Roper would pay them for the wheat and then into downtown Bakersfield the family would go to browse around the department stores and make its weekly purchases.

## History of Kern County

JOSEPH CUDA — In point of years of actual residence, it is doubtful if the celebrated Weed Patch of Kern County can boast an older settler than Joseph Cuda, who for a long period of useful activity has been a leading horticulturist of the locality and owns a finely improved ranch of eighty acres. The property and an adjacent tract of equal size were taken up by him as a homestead. Born near the city of Prague, Bohemia, June 28, 1864, Joseph Cuda was brought to America in infancy by his parents, John and Catherine (Pracil) Cuda.

The parents settled in Nebraska between Omaha and Lincoln and there two sons and a daughter were born. Having no means, the children were obliged to become self-supporting as soon as old enough and therefore had no educational advantages. The information Joseph Cuda now possesses has been acquired by observation, experience and reading.

Upon arriving in this state he settled on a farm in Kings County near Hanford, but a year later, in 1888, he came with his family to Kern County, where he took up a homestead of one hundred and sixty acres in the Weed Patch. At the end of seven years he proved up on the land, one-half of which he sold, retaining eighty acres for his own homestead. There are two children, Frank and Helen. The son is engaged as a driller of oil wells.

To have seen the Cuda farm in 1888 and not again until 1912, a stranger might have considered that a miracle had been wrought. But the only miracle is that of hard work, which has transformed the sage brush into a fine fruit farm. Beshides {sic} the valuable vineyard of four acres there is a tract of eight acres in figs now twenty years old, while during 1910 Mr. Cuda planted ten acres in the same Fruit. Twenty acres have been planted to peaches of the finest varieties. Of this peach orchard five acres were put out in 1907 and fifteen acres in 1908, the whole being now in thrifty bearing condition. The balance of the farm is in corn and alfalfa.

## How Weedpatch Was Named

We are grateful to Helen Cuda of East Bakersfield for the story of how Weedpatch got its name. Miss Cuda was born on the family farm near Vineland School and attended that school as a girl. Her father, Joseph Cuda, who was born in Bohemia in 1864 and came to the United States in 1869, homesteaded land east of Weedpatch in 1888. Mr. Cuda, who died December 30 1946, passed this story of the origin of Weedpatch on to this daughter.

pages.h: The family of Mary Kastl and Joseph Cuda
pages.t:
The name Weedpatch goes back to 1874 when that area was surveyed and located. The "weed patch" had been known many years before that to the Indians who camped there. Later when white settlers came to the area to raise grapes, figs, alfalfa, wheat, and barley, they grazed their cattle in the "weed patch." Farmers going after their cattle in the evening often visited with each other there and would say they had met in the "weed patch."

Mostly carrot weeds grew there and kangaroo rats, jack rabbits and cottontails lived in the weeds. A popular Sunday afternoon activity were the jack rabbit drives held there. The "weed patch" extended from east of the East Side Canal, which was completed in January 1893 by contractor E. M. Roberts, to DiGiorgie. It was six miles from north to south and four miles from east to west. The area provided excellent grazing when the dry season began in March. The weeds grew from two to four feet high, depending on the year's moisture.



### The family of Mary Kastl and Joseph Cuda

pages.h: The Family of Wenzel Kastl

## The Family of Wenzel Kastl

Wenzel Kastl was born 26 February 1831 in Vsepadly, Bohemia, house No. 11, the son of Thomas Kastl, and Maria, the daughter of Joseph Marsalek, a magistrate manager from Kosenice. Vsepadly is a village west and a little north of Klatovy. Wenzel was one of the seven sons of Thomas who came to America in the 1800s. We have not been able to find much about Wenzel; where he died, or was buried.

Wenzel married Barbara Blachnik in Bohemia. She died 14 August 1909 and was buried at St. Mary's Cemetery, Omaha, Nebraska.

Wenzel and Barbara came to the United States in 1867, arriving at the Port of Baltimore on October 2. They left from the Port of Bremen, Germany on the vessel Humbolt, ship's captain, Carl Gendes. The journey usually took from 2 to 3 weeks. Listed on the ship's records, as children of Wenzel Kastl, were John, age 6; Martin age 3; and Wenzel, age 6 months.

Douglas County Census records for 1880 show children of Wenzel and Barbara Kastl as: John 18, Martin 16, Mary 9, Anna 7, and Wenzel 2. Daughter Wilhelmina was born after 1880.

Wenzel Kastl had a homestead near Peter Kastl at Plasi, but went to Omaha sometime between 1870 and 1880.

Family records of Wenzel Kastl are incomplete. We were unable to trace descendants of his son John, or daughter Anna. They moved to the San Francisco area in the early 1900s, and contact was lost by other relatives.

pages.h: The Family of John Kastl
pages.t:
## The Family of John Kastl

John Kastl was born 29 November 1835 in Vsepadly, Bohemia, house No. 11, the son of Thomas Kastl, a farmer, and Maria, the daughter of Joseph Marselek, a magistrate manager from Kosenice. Thomas and Maria were farmers near the village of Vsepadly which is west and a little north of Klatovy. John was one of the seven sons who came to America in the 1800s. John died 20 December 1890, and was buried at Plasi, Saunders County, Nebraska.

John Kastl married Marie Kunes in Bohemia. She was born 23 August 1839, at Uboc which is very near Vsepadly. She was the daughter of Joseph Kunes and Susanna Janda. She died at the age of 94 at Vail, Iowa, 21 May 1934, and was buried at Plasi. She was living with her daughter Mrs. Mary Slegel at the time of her death.

John and Marie Kastl sailed from Bremen, Germany on the ship S.S Baltimore, arriving at the Port of Baltimore on the 14th of August 1872, with four children, Wenzel 8, Barbara 6, Anna 3, and Josef 11 months. The hard trip by sea usually took from 2 to 3 weeks.

It is not known if John and his family stopped in Chicago (ship records indicate that as destination) then went to Iowa, or Wisconsin before coming to Nebraska. It is believed that they may have gone at some time to either or both states.

It has not been verified, but Marie may have had a brother living in Wisconsin. It is not known just when the family arrived in Nebraska, but they did settle in Saunders County where John homesteaded 80 acres in Elk Precinct (west half of the southeast quarter of Section 30 in Township 15, North of Range 5 East). He applied for the homestead on 13 September 1872, at Lincoln, Nebraska, so he was in the state on that date. This land was near the site where the Sts. Cyril and Methodius Church is located (also known as Plasi).

They chose a site which reminded them of the rolling hills of their homeland in Bohemia on which to build their home and farm yard. All that remained of it in 1978 was the windmill. The grandchildren, however, recall the large fruit orchard, the gardens and beautiful flowers. In John's testimony in his Proof of Homestead dated 11 March 1879, he said:

"I am the head of a family consisting of a wife and seven children . . . I have cultivated about 50 acres of said land built a frame house 14x16 feet a comfortable dwelling having 1 door and 2 windows and built a granary 14x16 feet and a sod house and stable and have planted about 5 acres of forest trees and dug a well . . . have raised wheat, oats, corn, barley, rye, and vegetables."

John received his final certificate for the land on 13 March 1879. He also received his certificate of U.S Citizenship on 16 October 1878.

In addition to farming, John Kastl was the Postmaster of a station called Newton. This was actually on his farmstead which was used as a mail center for that area. Newton never became an incorporated village.

John lived on this farm until his death at age 55. Marie stayed on with her younger children for a few more years. She then lived for some time in the village of Bee, and then went to live with her daughter, Mrs. Slegel in Iowa, where she died at age 94.

Emporia Weekly Gazette (Kansas) 9 Mar. 1922

BORN IN AUSTRIA—HUNGARY;
Raised On A Western Farm (Mrs. Albert Mares)

Mrs. Albert Mares, who lives two miles from Emporia on East Logan Avenue, is an interesting and wholesome type of the foreign-born woman who never has discarded the Gospel of Work brought with her from her old home in Austria-Hungary but who, none the less, is a thorough American. She came with her parents to the prairies of Nebraska when she was 6 years old, and can recall that she had started to school in the old country, and that she brought with her her primer in the Bohemian language. And that is about all she can recall until the trip across seas, then the sod house on the prairie, in which her father and mother reared their large family.

As she grew up on the prairie farm, Mrs. Mares became early accustomed to hard, heavy toil. She could make a hand in the hay field, often she shocked wheat and husked corn, and after her marriage she helped her husband with the farm work. She went to school as occasion offered, but the Nebraska school terms were short in those days, and besides there was too much work to be done for little girls to find much time for school. She began working away from home when she was 12, and her wage was a dollar a week. There was mighty little play in her girlhood. SHe worked in various homes, "And I guess they liked me," she says, "as I never once was fired." When she was 15 she went to Lincoln to work in a big hotel as third cook, and within a year had become head cook.

Her wages as head cook were $30 a month, and the hotel did not keep union hours. All the women help of the hotel roomed together in a big room in the basement, and every morning at 4:30 a porter knocked on the door to waken them, and by 5 they were up and dressed. Breakfast started at 6 and lasted till 8, and by that hour it was time to begin preparations for the big noon dinner. Sometimes Mrs. Mares was through with

her part of the dinner work by 3 o'clock, sometimes by 4, but whatever the hour she finished her dinner work, she was in the kitchen at 5, and it was from 9 to 10 o'clock when the supper work was finished.

There were three cooks, six dining room girls, two ironers, a wash woman, two dishwashers, janitor, head waiter, bell boys, night and day porters—a small army of help. BUt it didn't take much to feed them, says Mrs. Mares, as the help was supposed to eat what was left when the paying guests were through, and sometimes it was mighty slim pickings. Often big special midnight suppers were served, and the help worked right through till all was finished, with no over time—but at such times they all had a big feed, as there was certain to be a lot of food left. The landlord kept an eye on the kitchen, usually, and there was no chance for the help to eat on the sly, as he was likely to bob in any minute.

The women help did their washing and sewing at night, in the little time they had left after their long day's work. And they did each others work, in turns, that all might have occasional opportunity to go to church.

"I might have held that job a long time," says Mrs. Mares, "but old country folks thought a girl must be married by the time she was 18, and so, at 18, I was married, in the same sod house on my parents' homestead in which they had started life on the prairie. My father had built a new house, of lumber, but they hadn't moved into it. My mother was afraid the wind would blow it away. My wedding dress was red changeable silk, with an overskirt, trimmed with black silk lace. A friend of mine helped me make it. I had bought a sewing machine while I was working, and learned to sew. My girls can all sew well, and are good housekeepers.

"Mr. Mares and I lived on a part of his father's land, but here again, everything was new, and the prairie was so bare. We built what we needed, a little four-room house, and when the other part of the farm was sold, we sold too. We lived several place in Nebraska, always trying to get ahead, always planning so that life might be better for our children than it had been for us. Some years we did well, and others it was hard work making a living, for we had to fight all the bad things that come to farmers."

Ten years ago the Mareses came to Lyon County to visit their daughter who, with her husband, lived on a farm near Miller. Also, they visited the Anton Ptaceks, who had been their neighbors in Nebraska. The Mareses liked Lyon County and after considerable looking around, they bought the old Laupheimer farm, of 170 acres. The winters are long and cold in Nebraska, and they felt they would like to live in a warmer climate. Here, they have met many discouragements in the way of dry weather and high water and all the ills that have hit Kansas farmers in the past nine years. But they wouldn't care to return to Nebraska, and they wouldn't consider leaving the farm. They wished to nearer schools and church and the location of the Laupheimer farm suited them exactly.

The Mareses went home to Nebraska after their visit, and the next spring came here to live. The new farm was badly run down, the house had burned a year or two earlier, many of the trees had been destroyed and the orchard had mostly died out. The family faced a big job of getting the place cleaned up, the soil into better producing condition, a new house, and all of the thousand and one things that confront thrifty farmers on a run-down place. A small house had been moved to the farm after the big house burned, and in this the family lived until 1917, when they built their present handsome, convenient residence.

Always Mrs. Mares has done a great deal of work on the farm, aside from her housekeeping and baby-tending. She has reared ten children, six daughters and four sons, and one baby died in infancy. Five of the daughters are married: the youngest, Lydia, was graduated from the Emporia High School last year, and the four sons, John, Joe, Adolph and Anton, run the farm. Mr. Mares has put out a new orchard, and spends much time with his trees. He hopes to have great deal of fruit on the place within the next few years, provided the late springs don't kill it.

"I couldn't be happy without my chickens and other poultry," says Mrs. Mares. "I make a lot of money off of them, too. Last year I raised 100 geese, 300 chickens, some turkeys, guineas and ducks, but geese and chickens are my principal poultry crop. I sell many eggs, too, though we probably eat more than we sell. My geese bring good prices, and I dress them and have the feathers for my own use. I have given each of my married daughters two featherbeds and six pillows, and I am making like outfits for my sons and for my daughter at home."

"Mother strips her feathers, too," said the daughter. Lydia, "and that makes them just like down." Mrs. Mares brought two boxes in which she ws preparing feathers for pillows. One box contained the striped feathers, light as down, indeed, and as soft and fluffy, the other box containing the spines of the feathers, carefully stripped of the down. Wonderful beds such feathers make, and wonderful is the patience that goes into the making of them.

"Mother furnished this house with her goose money," said Lydia, "and we buy so many things with poultry money that we have decided that poultry pays better than anything else on the farm. Mother puts in the greater part of her time with the poultry."

Lydia, since the marriage of the next youngest daughter, last year, has taken over a large part of the housekeeping.

Mrs. Mares had Rhode Island Red and White Leghorn chickens—a great egg and table combination.

pages.h: The family of Anna C. Mares and Joseph J. Pokorny
pages.t:
Her facilities for raising and caring for poultry are good—plenty of yards and coops and shade and water. Also she is a good butter-maker, and sells most of her product to regular customers the year round. The butter money pays for clothing and groceries and many other things that the women of the family need.

The Mareses profited by their oil lease more than anyone in their neighborhood, when there was oil excitement in this community a few years ago. They refused to lease at the low prices their neighbors were taking, and when it seemed certain the well being drilled on the farm of a neighbor would bring in oil, the promoters asked the Mareses their price, and they said $5000. The money was paid over to them so quickly it took their breath.

"That $5000 followed a year of bad crops," said Mrs. Mares, "and with it we built our house." If it hadn't come, we might still be living in the little four rooms. And then the well was a dry one—wasn't that a good joke on the oil men?"

It is a far cry from the sod house of her childhood, the ox teams of the early days in Nebraska, the long disances to town and school and church to the well-equipped conveniently located farm which now is the Mares home. "Yet we can't stop work," says Mrs. Mares, "and we wouldn't want to if we could." The new house has nine rooms, is modern except for heat, and the basement and all the rooms are ready for the installation of a furnace as soon as prices go down a little. The barn and milk house, as well as the residence, are lighted by electricity, and the farm has most of the modern farm conveniences.

Mrs. Mares believes strongly in education. She reads the newspapers and magazines, and is glad her children's opportunities have been better than hers were. She is a devoted Catholic, and says she has little time for going out except to church. BUt she likes to read about what other people in the world are doing, and keep informed as to the great world movements.

"My parents came to America." says Mrs. Mares, "as did so many old country people, to get their sons aways from the army. My father and mother had a hard time, and just as my life has been easier than was my mother's, so my children's life is easier than mine has been. It is hard for us old country people to learn new ways, and we are likely to think old ways the best. But we have to learn that what were the best ways in the old country are not always the best ways here. And the quicker we learn this, and apply it, the quicker we become happy and satisfied, instead of longing for the old country. My mother is still living, well along in the eighties. For years she was postmaster, the postoffice being in her little sod house. Always she wished for better things, and always she worked hard for the, and taught her children to work for them. She kept her children thinking of the church, too, as I have tried to keep mine. We can't be very bad if we love our church. I never have been sick—I think it is because I have been outdoors so much. I have worked any place on the farm I was needed, and have been glad I could do it, glad I had the strength to do it. I am proud of my good, strong boys and girls, and of our home and of all we have been able to accomplish."

And so ended a great lesson in practical Americanization. —Laura M. French.

## The family of Josef Kastl

Josef Kastl was born 15 January 1840 in Vsepadly, Bohemia, house No. 11, the son of Thomas Kastl, a farmer, and Maria, the daughter of Joseph Marselek, a magistrate manager from Kosenice. Thomas and Maria were farmers near the village of Vsepadly which is west and a little north Klatovy. Josef was one of the seven sons who came to America in the 1800s. Josef died in 1921 and was buried at Brainard, Nebraska.

Josef Kastl married Dorota Blaha in 1863 in Bohemia. She was born in 1833 in Bohemia, died in 1919 and was buried at Brainard.

Josef and Dorota sailed from Bremen, Germany on the ship S.S. Berlin, arriving at the Port of Baltimore on 22 April 1868, with two children, Mathias 3, and Theresia 9 months. The hard trip by sea usually took from 2 to 3 weeks. These two children died soon after arriving in Nebraska, and buried in Omaha.

## The family of Jacob Kastl

Jacob Kastl was born 5 May 1847 in Vsepadly, Bohemia, house No. 11, the son of Thomas Kastl and Maria, the daughter of Joseph Marselek, a magistrate manager from Kosenice. Thomas and Maria were farmers near the village of Vsepadly which is west and a little north of Klatovy. Jacob was one of the seven sons who came to America in the 1800s. Jacob died 28 February 1935 and was buried at Plasi, Saunders County, Nebraska.

Jacob Kastl married Alzbeta Nemecek, probably at her home in Lepadlech, Bohemia where a marriage contract was signed 31 January 1872. (Copy follows on another page) She was born 1849, daughter of Joseph Nemecek, died 28 March 1921, and was buried at Plasi.

Funeral of Jakub Kastl
Was in 87th year at the time of passing away.

Bruno, March 11, 1935—Funeral services were held from the Plasi Catholic church Monday, March 4, for Jakub (Grandpa) Kastl who passed away at the home of his son, Frank Kastl, Thursday, February 28, after an illness of two weeks duration. Rt. Rev. Msgr. Mlejnekof Weston made the funeral address and Rev. Father Cernik of Prague sang the Requiem Mass. The pallbearers were his four sons, John, Vincent, Frank, and Anton, and two nephews, Charles Kastl of Prague and Thomas Kastl of North Bend. Members of the K.D. Lodge, to which Mr. Kastl belonged, escorted the remains to the grave and little Christine Kastl carried the flowers. Interment was in the Plasi Cemetery.

Jakub Kastl, who was in his 87th year at time of death was born in Ouboc, Czechoslovakia, July 25, 1847, where he grew to manhood and where he was united in marriage to Alzbeta Nemecek in 1872. They emigrated to America — arriving in the United States and homesteading on a farm near Plasi, Saunders county, some three months later, where they resided for some time then moved to east Butler county.

Eleven children were born to Mr. and Mrs. Kastl, four of whom, Louis, Ann, Jake and Ed preceded their father in death. The surviving children are Mary (Mrs. V.A. Dobry) and John Kastl, both of Yukon, Okla., Vincent Kastl of Rising CIty {sic}, Frank Kastl of Bruno, Lizzie (Mrs. J.C. Rerucha) of Chicago, Ill., Anton Kastl of Yukon, Okla., and Antoinette (Mrs. Joseph Ratkovec) of Rising City. There are also 28 grandchildren and five great-grandchildren surviving Grandpa Kastl. Mrs. Kastl preceded her husband in death. Mr. Kastl had six brothers, Peter, Thomas, Joseph, Andrew, John, and Wencl, and one sister, Eva, all of whom passed away prior to the death of Grandpa Kastl.

Those in attendance at the funeral from elsewhere were Joseph Vrbka and family of Surprise, Mr. and Mrs. James Vech of Cedar Bluffs, Mr. and Mrs. Frank Fujan and son, James, and Mr.and Mrs. Thomas Kastl, all from North Bend, Mr. and Mrs. James J. Zima and Ed Krenk of Abie.

Grandpa Kastl, who passed away quietly at the home of his son, Frank, with whom he had made his home the past 23 years, was a devout Catholic. He was one of the founders of the first Catholic church at Plasi. Of cheerful disposition one of his pastimes in later years was singing. Being one of the early pioneers of the locality where he lived he had a wide circle of warm friends that enjoyed his companionship.

Cards of Thanks — We wish to express heartfelt thanks to Rt. Rev. Msgr. VictorMlejnek, Rev. B. Cernik members of the K.D. Lodge and the Plasi choir and also to those who attended the funeral in spite of bad weather. —John, Vincent, Frank, and Anton Kastl and Mrs. Joseph Ratkovec.

(Butler County Press)

MARRIAGE AGREEMENT

With Jacob Kastl son of Tomas[?] Kastl, a small farmer from Old Hutti[?], as first party and Joseph Nemecek, semi-large farmer from Lepadloch No. 49 , as father and fatherly guardian of his daughter Elizabeth Nemecek as second party. On this day and year between both parties agreement has been reached on all possessions and gifts given and secured and marriage was concluded, to which Elizabeth Nemecek consented to their matrimony as husband and wife with agreement as follows:

I. Both betrothed promise each other love and faithfulness and agree to the marriage contract and the rights they may have.

II. Bride Elizabeth Nemecek shall deliver to her groom Jacob Kastl 500zlatych(dollars) Five-hundred Zlatych, and for the wine value not known but when amount reaches that agreed upon, Father Joseph Nemecek on receipt will deliver to Groom Jacob Kastl the sum of 250 zlatych, Two-hundred-fifty Zlatych, with which to make preparations for a trip to America.

## The family of Thomas Kastl

Thomas Kastl was born 4 January 1850 in Vsepadly, Bohemia, house No. 11, the son of Thomas Kastl, a farmer, and Maria, the daughter of Joseph Marsalek, a magistrate manager from Kosenice. Thomas and Maria were farmers near the village of Vsepadly which is west and a little north of Klatovy. Thomas's mother died after the birth of her seventh son, Andrew. A few years later, probably at the suggestion of their older brother Peter, young Thomas and Andrew came to the United States, sailing from Bremen, Germany on the S.S Johannes—Wilhelmina, arriving at the Port of Baltimore on 29 May 1867.

Family records show that Thomas first went to Cedar Rapids, Iowa and then on to Champaign, Illinois.

In 1873, Thomas married Augusta Johns in Champaign. She was born in Poland, near Warsaw, and had come to Champaign to be with cousins. SHe died 1 May 1885. Thomas married Emma Fowler of Meredosia, Illinois on 21 February 1886. She was Pennsylvania German. She died 25 December 1896 with an infant son. Thomas Kastl died 30 September 1904. Although Thomas had 8 children, there are no surviving descendants.

pages.t:
## The family of Andrew Kastl

Andrew Kastl was born 27 November 1853 in Stara Hut, Bohemia, house No. 1, the son of Thomas Kastl and Maria, the daughter of Joseph Marsalek, a magistrate manager from Kosenice. Thomas and Maria were farmers near the village of Vsepadly which is west and a little north of Klatovy. Andrew was the last child of Maria who died soon after his birth. Andrew died 5 May 1906, and was buried at Plasi, Saunders County, Nebraska.

According to ship records, young Andrew and his brother Thomas arrived at the Port of Baltimore 29 May 1867 on the ship Johannes—Wilhelmine which sailed from Bremen, Germany.

He married Barbara Valecka. She was born in 1861, died in 1948 and buried at Plasi.

An article which describes Andrew's life, was printed in the Czech newspaper Katolika, published in Chicago probably in 1904.

### Andrew Kastl, West Nebraska, and his large family

Andrew Kastl was born in the old Country, Novo-Kdysky County, in the village of Oboc or the Old "Hut". His parents were very religious and rich. He soon had a misfortune. His mother died the next day of his birth. He was the fourteenth, and the last child born to the first maarriage, and never knew his mother. Her last words were: "Child, who is going to take care of you now?"

His father married again and there was big change. The little boy was neglected for 13 years. SO his father sent him to his brother Peter Kastl in America, in the year of 1867.

Andrew lived with his uncle for some time, and everybody knew that he didn't have it the best. 100 miles to the Mill, 18 miles to the Mail Box, and not much money.

Peter Kastl was the first settler in Saunders County. When Andrew grew up, Peter found him a job on the farm. He worked hard on the farm till he was 21 years old and the pay was small.

At that time he homesteaded some land, dug out a hole in the bank for his home, was batching and saving his money. He wasn't very happy living there alone, so he sold his property and moved to Wahoo. At that time there were only 15 houses in Wahoo. Soon he got into the Tavern business with a partner, who soon kicked him out. $700 was gone so he went to work on the farm again.

Times got better. People were moving in and price of land went up. He found a job at one Irish family (very religious) where he stayed for several years. Finally he settled on some school land with his brother Jakub, he loved much.

In the meantime a girl came from the old country and Andy married her. She is the mother of children you can see on the picture. They still live on the farm.

Andrew died 2 years ago, he was a good father, good catholic and he asked his children to never marry non-catholic if they want to be satisfied. They were all well off.

He was kind and was the county assessor for many years to the satisfaction of the citizens.

Lived in Nebraska since 1867 and had Life Insurance for $2600.

There were 7 brothers here. Two daughters are married; one to T. Rech and one to Joe Vrbka.

I hope that the rest will follow their sisters, mother and father, and will remember them.

Translated from Katolik, newspaper, Chicago, ILL. (probably 1904)

## Second Marriage of Tomas Kastl

### The family of Tomas Kastl and Barbara Kellner

Tomas Kastl, a widower, living in the village of Stara Hut, Bohemia, married Barbara Kellner 6 February 1855. He was 48 years old, she was 26. She was born 14 April 1828, daughter of Simon Kellner and Alzbeta Bauer. Their children:

1. ALZBETA — (b) 12 Nov. 1857. (d) 1 Dec. 1857.
2. MARIA (b) 5 May 1860 at Stara Hut, House No. 1.
3. FRANTISKA — (b) 29 Dec. 1862. (d) 4 Apr. 1869.
4. ANNA — (b) 12 Mar. 1865 at Stara Hut, House No. 3.
5. JOSEF — (b) 3 Aug. 1867 at Stara Hut, House No. 3
6. ALZBETA — (b) 20 Dec. 1869 at Stara Hut, House No. 3.

It is believed that none of these children came to America. The fourth daughter, Anna, who was a half-sister to the seven Kastl brothers who settled in America, married Joseph Zima in Bohemia, in 1887. James Zima, a son of Anna and Joseph, did come to the United States in 1922. He married, and has descendants in Nebraska.

pages.t:
## . . . and in Conclusion



After more than 5 years of searching for information about the Kastl family, both past and present, it was time to put some of it in print. It would have been wonderful to have been able to record every descendant of Thomas Kastl, but that is not possible. There are many names missing we know. The tremendous task of trying to contact members of this large family, scattered over the United States, would have taken a lifetime.

Others before us did have an interest in the family and devoted time and travel seeking and searching for Kastl family members. Vincent Kastl, son of Jacob, spent years of his life in this search. He died in 1970. Joseph Kastl, unfortunately unknown to us, also contracted some Kastl families in Nebraska some years ago, in the search of names. Calvin Kastl, in Kansas, came to Nebraska in 1982, hoping he could find a link to his family. Calvin died in 1983, and we have not yet been able to find the connection from Bohemia. We are sorry. And, we mourn our cousin Leslie Kastl from Weston, who died in 1984; he was a dovoted family enthusiast. He gave his time to family; and traveling, and doing what he could to get this book together.

With whatever flaws one may find in this book, we are happy to have spent our time on it, contacting our Kastl family members, and to have put this much into print. And, we will repeat: hopefully, there will be someone some day who may wish and be able to continue and expand this project.

—Evelyn Coufal, York Nebraska
—Francis Vech, Cedar Bluffs, Nebraska (June 1985)

pages.t: The Union Pacific shipping points were, successsively, Schuyler, Kearney, and Ogallala. Here the steers were driven up chutes into cattle cars which conveyed them to packers in Omaha and Chicago. (Photo from Nebraska—A Pictorial History) As homesteaders moved out on the plains, the cattle trails were pushed westward. The days of the Long Drive came to an end in the mid-1880s when expanding settlement blocked the trails and homesteaders invoked herd laws to keep the cattle out.

## Kastl's Family Supplementary Section

### Josef Kastl Log House — Page 8 Addition

Josef first came to Omaha where he was a stone mason. To raise money for his family, he worked for the Union Pacific Railroad building station houses through Nebraska and Wyoming.

When he returned to Omaha, he equipped a wagon pulled by a tean {sic} of oxen, and went to homestead west of Omaha, in Newman Precinct, Saunders County.

He proceeded to build a log cabin, but in the meantime lived with his wife in a nearby cave dug into the side of a hill.

A missionary priest on horseback would periodically visit Josef's cabin and say Mass, using a table that is still in the family.
